issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a 19-year-old male with stalking trauma, body-focused shame is hard to reconcile unless there was physical or sexual assault. With the given trauma type, this item is clinically incongruent and stands out from the other appraisal items, which are otherwise plausible for stalking.

issues.item: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless the stalker was also a trusted person. Because trauma type has already been fixed as stalking and no other node supplies context supporting an intimate or trusted-perpetrator stalking scenario, this item is clinically questionable in this profile.

issues.item: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' can fit only if the stalker was a trusted person, but the profile gives no other items in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies to support an interpersonal-betrayal formulation. Paired with global characterological self-blame, this creates a specific relational-trauma narrative that is not otherwise represented in the self-report.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is not impossible, but it implies the stalker was a trusted close other. The rest of the profile provides no supporting items in Memory, Threat, Triggers, or Strategies, and with no active formulation edges this appraisal stands as an unsupported trauma-specific claim. The other appraisal items ('I have to be on guard all the time', 'The world is a dangerous place') fit stalking more generically, but the betrayal item makes the node less coherent as a standalone set.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: These two items are not negative appraisals in the usual cognitive sense; they describe ongoing threat monitoring/safety behavior rather than evaluative beliefs. With a formulation showing no active edges and only the Negative Appraisals node populated, selecting predominantly hypervigilance/vigilance items makes the node content misaligned with the intended construct.

vignette:
Kofi is a 19-year-old UX designer who came to therapy at the urging of his supervisor, after several months of declining performance and increasing isolation at work. He is single, of West African descent, and lives alone in a studio apartment in a midsized city. He completed the PCL-5 with a score of 65, and during the initial sessions, he described a single traumatic event that had reshaped his entire sense of safety.

The event occurred about ten months ago, during his final semester of a design bootcamp. Kofi had been working late nights on a capstone project, often alone in the co-working space where his cohort met. A fellow student-a woman he had exchanged only a few polite words with-began to wait for him outside the building. At first, it seemed coincidental. Then she started leaving notes on his desk, commenting on things he had said in casual conversation, referencing details about his schedule that he had never told her. Over three weeks, it escalated. She found his personal email, sent him long messages about how they were meant to be together, and began appearing at the coffee shop he visited every morning. Kofi reported feeling a creeping dread he could not name at the time. He told himself he was overreacting. He did not want to cause trouble. He kept being polite, hoping she would lose interest. One night, she followed him to his bus stop, grabbed his arm, and told him she knew where he lived. He pulled away and ran. The next day, he reported her to the program director. She was expelled, and a restraining order was filed. But by then, Kofi had already stopped sleeping.

In the months that followed, the world had become, in his words, "a dangerous place." He described this not as an abstract belief but as a felt certainty that lived in his body. Every time he left his apartment, he scanned the street for anyone who looked like they might be watching him. He checked the faces of women in his vicinity with a hypervigilance that exhausted him. He had come to believe that the event happened because of the way he acted-because he had been too nice, too accommodating, too afraid of being rude. He was certain that if he had been firmer earlier, or if he had not smiled at her that first time she said hello, none of it would have happened. This self-blame sat inside him like a verdict: he had brought this on himself, and therefore he could not trust his own judgment about who was safe.

As a UX designer, Kofi now works in an open-plan office with low cubicle walls and a constant flow of collaborators walking past his desk. He had always enjoyed the energy of the space, but after the stalking, he found himself unable to focus. He had to be especially careful-he was certain that you never know what can happen next. He began to sit with his back to the wall, his laptop angled so that no one could see his screen. He stopped wearing headphones because he needed to hear footsteps approaching. He started coming in early and leaving late, timing his movements to avoid the crowd at the elevator. His supervisor noticed that he had stopped attending team stand-ups and was communicating only by Slack. When asked about it, Kofi said he was "just busy." In truth, he was terrified of the small talk, of the possibility that a colleague might ask him a personal question, of the vulnerability of being known.

Over the weeks and months, Kofi's avoidance had taken on a pattern that he could no longer ignore. He had stopped going to the grocery store after dark. He had deleted his social media accounts. He had stopped dating entirely-the idea of someone having access to his life, his routines, his home address felt unbearable. His only social contact was with his mother, who he called once a week, and even then he kept the conversations short and vague. The consequence that finally brought him to therapy was occupational: he had missed three project deadlines, and his supervisor had placed him on a performance improvement plan. Kofi was terrified of losing his job, not just because of the income but because his apartment, his routine, his carefully controlled environment was the only place he felt even remotely safe. He came to the first session with his hands clasped tightly in his lap, and he asked, almost immediately, whether the therapist would need to record anything. He said he was hoping to feel less afraid, but what he did not say-what he could not yet articulate-was that he was also terrified of what would happen if he let his guard down. Because if the world really was as dangerous as he now believed, then his vigilance was not a symptom. It was the only thing keeping him alive.
